name: The Breakup Scene
blurb: A couple packs up their flat calmly, until one small kitchen clock says everything
title: The Breakup Scene: 2-Person Drama Script for Acting Practice
description: A 4-minute drama duet for 2 actors of any gender: a couple splits calmly over a clock that runs ten minutes fast. Free to perform, film and record.
h1: The Breakup Scene: a 4-Minute Drama Script for 2 Actors
logline: Riley and Jordan are packing up the flat they shared for six years, politely, carefully, without a single raised voice. The only thing they cannot agree on is a cheap kitchen clock that Jordan set ten minutes fast on the day they moved in.
setting: A small kitchen half packed into boxes, early evening. Props: a cheap wall clock, cardboard boxes, packing tape, a few mugs and newspaper, a door key.

roles.name: Riley
roles.note: 25 to 40, any gender. Has already decided to leave and wants to go without a fight, but still loves Jordan.

roles.name: Jordan
roles.note: 25 to 40, any gender. Organised, always planning the next thing. Wants this to stay tidy so it does not have to hurt.

script.scene: INT. KITCHEN OF A SMALL FLAT – EARLY EVENING

script.action: Half-packed boxes everywhere. A cheap round clock on the wall. RILEY wraps mugs in newspaper. JORDAN comes in with a roll of tape.

script.say: I've done the books. Yours are by the door. I put the cookbook in your box.
It's yours. You bought it.
You're the one who cooks.
Fine.

script.action: Jordan tapes a box shut. Glances up at the clock.

script.say: The van's at seven. So really ten to.
So really seven.
Don't.
I'm just saying. It's ten minutes fast.
I know it's ten minutes fast. I set it.
Six years ago.
And it works. We have never once missed a train.
We've never missed anything. You make sure of it.
Is that a crime now?
No. It's just the way you look at it. Every evening. Like it's counting down.

script.action: Silence. Jordan reaches up and takes the clock off the wall.

script.say: Do you want it?
The clock?
It's half yours.
Keep it.
You hate it. That's why you won't take it.
I don't hate it. I hate that with you I'm always living ten minutes from now.
What does that even mean?

We hadn't unpacked this flat and you were looking at bigger ones. I got the job I wanted and you asked me what the next one was. I tell you I'm happy, and you ask if I'll still be happy in five years.
That's called caring about the future.
It's called never being here. I'm here, Jordan. I've always been right here. You just kept running ahead to check I'd still be coming.
So it's the clock.
It's not the clock.
No. It's never the clock.
Do you remember the day we hung it? You stood on the chair and I held the chair.
You said, if we're always ten minutes early, nothing bad can ever catch up with us.
I said that?
You did. I thought it was the sweetest thing I'd ever heard.
And now?
Now I think you were scared. And I think you still are.

script.action: Jordan sets the clock face up on a box between them.

script.say: I could set it right. Tonight. Look. Ten minutes back and it's done.
Don't.
Why not?
Because you'd do it for me. And in a month you'd be ahead again, and you'd hate yourself for it, and I'd hate watching.
You've thought about this a lot.
About a year.
A year. And I thought I was the one who planned ahead.
What happened a year ago?

Nothing. That's the thing. It was a Sunday. You were reading flat listings in bed and I was watching the rain, and I thought, this is perfect. I turned to tell you, and you said, what about Thursday for a viewing?
You could have said it anyway.
I know. I stopped saying things. That part is on me.

script.action: Riley tapes the last box and lifts it.

script.say: Can I ask you something? Were you ever going to tell me before you'd decided?
I tried. You were always already in the next conversation.

script.action: Jordan nods. Riley puts a door key on the box, next to the clock.

script.say: I'll send on your post.
Thank you.
And if you want the clock later, just say. I can drop it round, it's no trouble, I'll be passing that way anyway on—
Jordan. It was never fast.
What?
The clock. I put it right every night after you fell asleep. Six years. You were never early. You were always exactly on time.
Why would you do that?
Because you needed to feel early. And I needed you to actually be here.

script.action: Riley goes. The door closes. Jordan looks at the clock for a long moment, then slowly turns the hand ten minutes forward. Stops. Turns it back. Lights down.

ul: Keep the space small: two or three boxes centre, a chair, and the clock on a wall or a hook upstage so the audience can see it all scene. A door or an exit on one side is the only way out.
Start both actors busy with their hands. Packing is the shield; the scene changes the moment someone stops packing.
Jordan taking the clock off the wall is the first big move. Place the clock on the box exactly between the two actors so it becomes the third person in the room.
Riley should be at the door, box in arms, for the last exchange. Distance makes the reveal quieter and harder.

For a self-tape, film it as a two-shot from one corner with a reader off camera, or shoot each actor separately in a close single. For audio, add the sound of tape tearing and newspaper rustling so the listener feels the packing.
Nobody shouts. The tension comes from two people being polite on purpose. If you feel the urge to raise your voice, lower it.
Riley plays kindness, not victory. Riley is leaving because of love that ran out of room, not because Jordan is bad.
Jordan plays control. Every practical line about the van, the post or the books is an attempt to keep the feeling at arm's length. Let it crack only on the almost-laugh about planning ahead.
Take a real pause before It was never fast. Riley is deciding whether to say it at all.
The last action is the whole ending. Jordan should move the hand forward out of habit, then understand, then turn it back. Do not rush it and do not cry on cue; let the audience fill it in.
Change the object: a car that is always kept on a full tank, a calendar filled months ahead, a phone alarm that goes off early. Keep the secret correction at the end.
Play it as two old friends ending a shared business or two flatmates moving out; the clock works just as well when the love is not romantic.
Write a part two set a year later, when Jordan turns up on time, exactly on time, at Riley's new door.

prompts.keyframe: Small kitchen at early evening, warm low lamp light, cardboard boxes and newspaper-wrapped mugs, two adults packing in silence on opposite sides, a cheap round wall clock between them in focus, cinematic still, 16:9, muted colours.
shots: Medium two-shot, static camera, two adults pack boxes in a quiet kitchen, one glances up at a wall clock, polite and tense mood, warm evening light.
Close-up on hands taking a round clock off the wall and placing it on a cardboard box, slow push-in, heavy silence.
Wide shot from inside the kitchen, one person at the open door holding a box speaks gently, the other freezes by the clock, still camera, bittersweet mood.
Close-up of a person alone turning the hand of a clock forward, pausing, then turning it back, slow dolly in, soft lamp light, lights fade.

faq.q: Can I use The Breakup Scene for an audition or on a monetised channel?
faq.a: Yes. The script is original and released under CC BY 4.0, so you can perform, film, record and post it, including on monetised channels and in competitions. Just credit Script: cv.cm.

faq.q: How long does it run and how should we rehearse it?
faq.a: About 4 minutes with natural pauses. Run it first as a pure table read, then once with only the packing actions and no words, so the business is easy before you add the lines.

faq.q: Does the clock reveal make sense if Jordan never noticed?
faq.a: Yes, and actors can play it: Jordan always trusted the clock and never checked it, which is exactly the point. Jordan believed in being early so much that being on time felt like being early.
